toc_content:
Databases — Postgres especially. SQL is non-negotiable. pgvector for embeddings.
Concurrency, caching, queues, retries, idempotency
Git, code review, CI/CD
System design — how a real backend is structured
2. LLM API mastery
Multiple providers: Claude, GPT, Gemini, plus an open model (Llama, Qwen, Mistral)
Streaming, function calling, structured output (JSON mode, Pydantic + instructor)
Prompt caching, batching, rate-limit handling
Multi-turn conversation state management
Reasoning / extended thinking modes — when worth the cost
Token economics: counting, trimming, why context length matters
3. Evaluation
The skill that separates seniors from juniors in this role.
Building eval sets from real or synthetic data
LLM-as-judge: when it works, when it lies, pairwise > absolute
Regression testing on every prompt change
Production observability — Langfuse, LangSmith, Helicone, Braintrust
Closing the loop: production traces → eval set → improvements
4. RAG architectures
Embedding models, vector DBs (start with pgvector)
Chunking strategies — the part most people get wrong
Hybrid search (dense + BM25), reranking
Query transformation, metadata ﬁltering
Citations and grounding
5. Agents and tool use
Function calling fundamentals
ReAct, planning, control ﬂow
MCP (Model Context Protocol)
When not to build an agent — usually a deterministic pipeline is better6. Production concerns
Cost engineering: model routing, caching, prompt compression
Latency: streaming, speculative decoding, time-to-ﬁrst-token
Safety: prompt injection defense, output moderation, PII handling
Deployment: Docker, FastAPI, a cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure), serverless
Self-hosting basics: vLLM, Ollama, when to bring inference in-house
7. Just enough ML literacy
What pretraining, post-training, ﬁne-tuning, and RLHF/DPO mean
Tokenization, embeddings, transformers at intuition level
Fine-tuning with LoRA when prompting hits its ceiling
Knowing what's possible — you'll be the AI subject expert on your team
8. Product and communication
Often the actual diﬀerentiator at hiring time.
Translating fuzzy product requirements into evaluable specs
Explaining capabilities and limits to non-technical stakeholders
Knowing when LLMs are not the right tool
The learning path
Months 1–2: Foundations
Solidify Python and backend engineering. Build a non-AI CRUD app with FastAPI,
Postgres, tests, Docker. This is your baseline.
LLM fundamentals: tokens, embeddings, transformers (intuition, not math). Karpathy's
Let's build GPT once.
Get ﬂuent with one frontier API end-to-end (recommend Claude or GPT). Streaming, tools,
structured output, error handling.
Project: A useful CLI or web tool you'd actually use. Code reviewer, meeting summarizer,
document Q&A — something concrete.
Months 2–4: RAG and agents
Build a real RAG system. Use pgvector. Implement chunking, hybrid search, reranking,
citations. Build the eval set ﬁrst.
